blocks.markdown:
Today's big question: what is in the sky, and why do we have day and night?

We will meet the Sun, the planets and the Moon.
blocks.say: Welcome, sky watcher! Today we have a big question. What is up there in the sky, and why do we have day and night? We will meet the Sun, the planets and the Moon, and learn how the Moon helps Muslims know when a new month begins. This is a game, not a test. Let's go!

blocks.alt: The Sun, planets and Moon are all in the sky.
blocks.caption: The Sun, planets and Moon are all in the sky.

terms.meaning: Everything we see above us when we look up.

blocks.markdown:
The **Sun** is a **star**. It gives us light and heat.

The Sun is much bigger than the Earth.
blocks.say: Look up in the daytime and you will see the Sun. The Sun is a star. It is a giant, glowing ball of hot gas. It is much, much bigger than the Earth. The Sun gives us light and warmth. Without it, Earth would be dark and freezing. But remember, never look straight at the Sun, because it can hurt your eyes.

blocks.alt: The Sun is a star that gives us light and heat.
blocks.caption: The Sun is a star that gives us light and heat.

blocks.markdown: Never look straight at the Sun. It can hurt your eyes.

A **planet** is a big ball that goes around a star.

There are **eight** planets that go around the Sun.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
blocks.say: Our Earth is a planet. A planet is a big round ball that goes around a star. Our Sun has eight planets going around it. In order from the Sun they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. Jupiter is the biggest planet.

scenes.say: Close to the Sun are four small rocky planets. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Earth is our home.

scenes.say: Further away are the four giants. Jupiter is the biggest. Saturn has beautiful rings. Then Uranus and Neptune, far, far away.

blocks.answer_markdown: **Jupiter** is the biggest planet. It is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it!

blocks.text: Stop 1: Why do we have day and night?

blocks.markdown:
The Earth **spins** round once every 24 hours.

The side facing the Sun has **day**. The side turned away has **night**.
blocks.say: Why is it light in the day and dark at night? The Earth is always spinning, like a top. It takes about twenty-four hours, one whole day, to spin all the way round. The side of the Earth facing the Sun has daytime. The side turned away from the Sun has night time. As Earth spins, our side moves into the light, and then back into the dark.

scenes.caption: Morning: our side meets the light.
scenes.say: Here is the Earth, with the Sun on the left. Watch it spin slowly. This is morning, and our side is just coming into the light.

scenes.caption: Noon: our side faces the Sun.
scenes.say: Now it is noon. Our side faces the Sun. It is the middle of the day!

scenes.caption: Evening: our side turns away.
scenes.say: The Earth keeps spinning. Now our side is turning away from the Sun. The evening is here.

scenes.caption: Night: our side faces away from the Sun.
scenes.say: Now it is the middle of the night. Our side is facing away from the Sun. Everything is dark. By morning, the Earth will have spun round again.

question.explanation: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.

blocks.text: Stop 2: The Sun's journey across the sky

blocks.markdown:
The Sun **rises** in the east and **sets** in the west.

Your shadow is long in the morning and evening, and short at noon.
blocks.say: Here is something to notice. In the morning, the Sun rises in the east. At lunchtime, it is high in the sky. Then in the evening, it sets in the west. Of course, it is really the Earth that is spinning. Shadows change too. In the morning and evening your shadow is long. At noon, when the Sun is high, it is short.

blocks.alt: The Sun rises in the east in the morning and sets in the west in the evening.
blocks.caption: The Sun rises in the east in the morning and sets in the west in the evening.

blocks.markdown:
The **Moon** is a ball of rock that goes around the Earth.

The Moon does not make its own light. It reflects light from the Sun.
blocks.say: At night we can often see the Moon. The Moon is not a star, and it is not a planet. It is a giant ball of rock that travels around the Earth. The Moon does not make its own light. It looks bright because it bounces back light from the Sun, like a mirror.

scenes.caption: The Moon goes around the Earth.
scenes.say: Here is the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. The Moon travels around the Earth.

scenes.caption: The Sun lights half of the Moon.
scenes.say: The Sun lights up one half of the Moon, like a torch lighting a ball. That is why the Moon seems to shine.

question.hint: It reflects light from the Sun.
question.explanation: The Moon reflects the light of the Sun.

blocks.markdown:
The Moon looks different shapes: **new moon**, **crescent**, half moon and **full moon**.

It goes through all its shapes in about one month.
blocks.say: Have you ever noticed that the Moon looks different on different nights? Some nights it is a thin curve, called a crescent. Some nights it is half. Some nights it is a big full circle, called a full moon. And on one night it is dark and we cannot see it at all, called a new moon. The Moon goes through all its shapes in about one month.

scenes.caption: New moon: we cannot see it.
scenes.say: It starts as a new moon. The Moon is there, but we cannot see it because its lit side faces away from us.

scenes.caption: A crescent moon.
scenes.say: A few days later we see a thin curve of light. This is a crescent moon. It is getting bigger.

scenes.caption: A half moon.
scenes.say: A week later it is half lit, like a half moon.

scenes.caption: A full moon.
scenes.say: Soon it is a big bright circle. This is a full moon!

scenes.caption: Back to a thin crescent.
scenes.say: Then it shrinks again, back to a thin crescent, and then a new moon. And it starts all over again.

blocks.text: Stop 1: A calendar that follows the Moon

blocks.markdown:
The **Islamic calendar** follows the Moon and has twelve months.

A new month starts when the new **crescent** moon is seen.
blocks.say: Muslims use a special calendar called the Islamic calendar. It follows the Moon. It has twelve months. Each month has twenty-nine or thirty days. A new month starts when the new crescent moon is seen in the sky. That is why people look at the sky when a month is about to end.

blocks.alt: A new month begins when the new crescent moon is seen.
blocks.caption: A new month begins when the new crescent moon is seen.

question.prompt: How many months are in the Islamic calendar?

blocks.markdown:
**Muharram** is the first month. **Ramadan** is the ninth month.

Eid ul-Fitr is at the start of Shawwal. Eid ul-Adha is in Dhul Hijjah, the twelfth month.
blocks.say: Here are the twelve Islamic months in order. The first month is Muharram. The ninth month is Ramadan, the month of fasting. The tenth month is Shawwal. Eid ul-Fitr is on the first day of Shawwal. The twelfth month is Dhul Hijjah, when the Hajj happens, and Eid ul-Adha is in this month.

blocks.say: Here are the first six months. Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi al-Thani, Jumada al-Awwal and Jumada al-Thani.

blocks.say: And the last six. Rajab, Shaban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Qadah and Dhul Hijjah.

blocks.text: Stop 3: Why we look for the crescent

blocks.markdown: People look for the new crescent to know when a month begins.
blocks.say: Why do families go outside to look for the new crescent? Because it tells us a new month is starting. At the end of Shaban, people look for the new crescent to see if Ramadan has begun. And at the end of Ramadan, they look for the new crescent to see if it is Eid! Let us think about it.

blocks.caption: A new crescent moon shows that a new month is beginning.

blocks.prompt: Why do people look for the new crescent moon at the end of a month?
blocks.answer_markdown: Because the new crescent moon shows that a **new Islamic month** is about to begin.
